questions.question: Why is base62 encoding preferred over base10 for generating short URL codes?
options: Base62 is faster to compute than base10
Base62 produces shorter codes because it has a larger character set
Base62 is more secure and prevents URL guessing
Base62 encoding is required by HTTP standards
questions.explanation: Base62 uses 62 characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) instead of 10 digits. This means a 7-character base62 code can represent 62^7 (~3.5 trillion) values, whereas a 7-digit base10 number only represents 10 million values. Shorter codes mean shorter URLs.

questions.question: In a URL shortener handling 100M new URLs per day with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, what is the approximate read QPS?
options: About 1,200 requests per second
About 12,000 requests per second
About 100,000 requests per second
About 1,000,000 requests per second
questions.explanation: 100M writes/day = ~1,157 writes/sec. With a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, reads are ~11,570/sec, approximately 12,000 QPS. This read-heavy pattern makes caching extremely valuable.

questions.question: What HTTP status code should a URL shortener return when redirecting a user to the original URL?
options: 200 OK with the original URL in the body
301 Moved Permanently or 302 Found
404 Not Found if the URL has expired
204 No Content with a Location header
questions.explanation: A 301 (permanent redirect) or 302 (temporary redirect) with a Location header is the standard approach. 301 lets browsers cache the redirect, reducing server load. 302 forces each request through the server, which is better for analytics tracking.

questions.question: Why is caching especially effective for a URL shortener service?
options: URL mappings change frequently and need fast updates
The service is read-heavy and URL mappings are immutable once created
Caching reduces the cost of base62 encoding computations
It prevents hash collisions in the shortening algorithm
questions.explanation: URL shorteners are heavily read-biased (10:1 or more). Once a short-to-long URL mapping is created, it never changes. This immutability makes it a perfect cache candidate — no cache invalidation complexity, and the 80/20 rule means caching popular URLs handles most traffic.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of using a pre-generated key service instead of hashing URLs on the fly?
options: It reduces storage requirements by 50%
It eliminates collision handling entirely since all codes are pre-verified unique
It makes the system stateless and easier to scale
It allows the system to work without a database
questions.explanation: A key generation service pre-generates unique codes and stores them in a pool. When a new URL arrives, it simply grabs the next available code. Since all codes were verified unique at generation time, there's zero collision risk during writes — simplifying the write path significantly.

questions.question: For a URL shortener storing 180 billion records at 500 bytes each, which database type is most appropriate and why?
options: A relational database like PostgreSQL for ACID transactions
A NoSQL key-value store like DynamoDB for simple lookups at massive scale
A graph database like Neo4j for relationship traversals
An in-memory database like Redis as the sole data store
questions.explanation: URL shorteners perform simple key-value lookups (short_code -> original_url) with no complex joins or transactions needed. A NoSQL key-value store like DynamoDB scales horizontally to handle 90TB+ of data and high throughput, making it ideal for this access pattern.

questions.question: When using MD5 hashing to generate short codes, what is the best strategy for handling collisions?
options: Increase the hash output length until collisions stop
Append a counter to the input and rehash until a unique code is found
Use a distributed lock to prevent concurrent writes
Switch to SHA-256 which never produces collisions
questions.explanation: When a collision occurs, appending an incrementing counter to the original URL and rehashing produces a new candidate code. This is retried until a unique code is found. While SHA-256 has fewer collisions than MD5, all hash functions can collide when truncated to 7 characters.

questions.question: A URL shortener uses 7-character base62 codes. After 5 years, 180 billion codes are used. What percentage of the total code space is consumed?
options: About 0.5%
About 5%
About 50%
About 95%
questions.explanation: The total base62 code space for 7 characters is 62^7 = ~3.52 trillion. Using 180 billion codes consumes 180B / 3.52T = ~5.1%. This leaves ample room for growth, which is why 7 characters is a safe choice for this scale.

questions.question: In a distributed URL shortener, two servers simultaneously try to shorten different long URLs and generate the same short code. How should the system handle this race condition?
options: Use optimistic locking: the first write wins, the second detects the conflict and retries with a new code
Use a global mutex lock on the entire database to serialize all writes
Accept duplicate mappings and resolve them during reads
Partition servers so no two servers can generate the same code range
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking with retry is the best approach. The database enforces uniqueness on the short_code column. If a concurrent insert fails due to a duplicate key, the server generates a new code and retries. A global lock would destroy write throughput at scale.

questions.question: You choose 301 (permanent) redirects for your URL shortener. A customer later wants to update the destination URL for an existing short code. What problem does this create?
options: The database schema doesn't support URL updates
Browsers and CDNs have cached the old 301 redirect and won't check the server again
The base62 code becomes invalid after modification
The cache eviction policy conflicts with 301 semantics
questions.explanation: A 301 tells browsers the redirect is permanent, so they cache it indefinitely and never re-check the server. If you update the destination URL in the database, users with cached 301s still go to the old URL. Use 302 (temporary) redirects if destination URLs may change.
